title: ARIA Roles, States, and Properties
summary: ARIA fills the gaps native HTML can't cover, but only if you keep its attributes in sync with the real UI. Learn the roles/states/properties model, the first rule of ARIA, and where staleness silently breaks the whole contract.

slides.markdown:
[Semantic HTML](semantic-html-for-a11y) gives you correct accessibility behavior automatically. ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) exists for the cases HTML doesn't cover natively — there's no `<tabs>` element, no built-in `<combobox>` with the exact keyboard behavior a design calls for, so a custom widget needs ARIA attributes to describe itself to the accessibility tree the way a native element would on its own.

The defining trade-off of ARIA: it's a **promise, not a guarantee**. Adding `role="button"` tells assistive tech "treat this as a button," but the browser doesn't verify the element actually behaves like one — no automatic keyboard handling comes with it. Every behavior a native element gives for free, ARIA requires you to implement and, critically, keep in sync with reality by hand.

This topic covers the roles/states/properties model, the common patterns, and the staleness bug that breaks more ARIA implementations in production than any other mistake.

slides.subTitle: Don't use it if a native element already works
slides.markdown:
The WAI-ARIA spec itself states this directly, and it's worth quoting because it's routinely ignored: **"No ARIA is better than bad ARIA."** If a native HTML element or attribute already has the accessibility semantics and behavior you need, use it instead of re-purposing a generic element with ARIA.

The reasoning: a native element's behavior is implemented and tested once, by browser vendors, across every assistive technology combination that exists. An ARIA-plus-div reimplementation has to get role, every relevant state, keyboard handling, and focus management all correct — and keep them correct as the component evolves — with none of the built-in safety net a native element has.

`role="button"` on a `<div>` is a common violation of this rule when `<button>` was sitting right there and would have needed zero extra code. Reach for ARIA specifically for the gaps HTML has no native answer for — that's the entire justification for its existence, not a general enhancement layer to sprinkle on everything.

| Category | What it describes | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Role** | what kind of thing this is — set once, rarely changes | `role="dialog"`, `role="tablist"` |
| **State** | current condition, expected to change during use | `aria-expanded`, `aria-checked`, `aria-disabled` |
| **Property** | a characteristic more fixed than a state, but not the role itself | `aria-label`, `aria-describedby`, `aria-required` |

The practical distinction that matters most: **states are the ones you must remember to update as the UI changes.** A role, once set, typically doesn't need to change for the component's lifetime — a dialog stays `role="dialog"` whether it's open or closed. A state like `aria-expanded` is meaningless the moment it stops tracking the real UI — `aria-expanded="false"` on a dropdown that's visibly open isn't a minor inaccuracy, it's actively wrong information being fed to a screen reader user who can't see that the div is visually expanded.

slides.subTitle: dialog, tablist/tab/tabpanel, alert
slides.markdown:
A handful of roles cover the majority of custom widgets that need them:

- **`role="dialog"`** (or `alertdialog` for one requiring immediate attention) — a modal or non-modal overlay; must be paired with `aria-modal="true"` for true modals and a label via `aria-labelledby` pointing at the dialog's heading.
- **`role="tablist"`/`"tab"`/`"tabpanel"`** — a tab interface; the selected tab needs `aria-selected="true"` and the corresponding panel needs to be associated via `aria-controls`, with unselected panels hidden.
- **`role="alert"`** — a self-announcing region for urgent, time-sensitive messages (a failed form submission, a connection drop); content injected into an element with this role gets announced by screen readers immediately, without the user needing to navigate to it — powerful, and easy to overuse for non-urgent updates where it becomes an interruption rather than a help.

Each role comes with an implicit contract about which states/properties must accompany it — `role="tab"` without `aria-selected` anywhere is an incomplete implementation, not a valid minimal one.

slides.sectionTitle: State that must stay in sync
slides.subTitle: aria-expanded, aria-hidden, aria-live
slides.markdown:
Three states show up constantly and each has a specific failure mode if it's set once and forgotten:

- **`aria-expanded`** — on a toggle control (a dropdown trigger, an accordion header), reflects whether the controlled content is currently shown. Must flip on every open/close, not just on initial render.
- **`aria-hidden="true"`** — removes an element and its descendants from the accessibility tree entirely, even though they remain visible and clickable in the DOM. A dangerous one to leave stale: applying it to a modal's background content while the modal is open is correct; forgetting to remove it after the modal closes makes the entire rest of the page invisible to a screen reader user with no visual indication anything is wrong.
- **`aria-live="polite"`** (or `"assertive"` for urgent cases) — marks a region whose content changes should be announced automatically when they change, without requiring focus to move there. Essential for things like a live-updating error count or a "3 new messages" badge.

All three are only correct at the instant they're set — the whole category is defined by needing to track the real, current UI state, not a fixed configuration choice made once.

slides.sectionTitle: A dropdown's ARIA mapped to its visual states
slides.markdown:
A custom dropdown has two visual states — closed and open — and each one requires a specific, different set of ARIA attributes on the trigger and the menu, not a single fixed set applied once at mount.

Closed state: trigger has `aria-expanded="false"`, `aria-haspopup="listbox"`; the menu itself is either removed from the DOM or has `hidden`/`aria-hidden="true"` applied, and is not part of the tab order. Open state: trigger flips to `aria-expanded="true"`; the menu becomes visible, its `hidden`/`aria-hidden` is removed, and its currently-highlighted option (if using roving focus rather than moving actual DOM focus) carries `aria-activedescendant` pointing at the highlighted item's id.

The attributes that must change between these two states are exactly the ones a naive implementation forgets to toggle — set once at mount and never touched again as the user opens and closes the menu.

![Dropdown closed vs open states with aria-expanded and aria-activedescendant](assets/dropdown-aria-states.svg)

assets.alt: Dropdown closed vs open states with aria-expanded and aria-activedescendant

slides.markdown:
The single most common real-world ARIA bug: an attribute is set correctly at the moment a component is built and tested, then silently goes wrong the first time the UI updates through a code path the original author didn't consider — a dropdown closed by clicking outside it, say, rather than by clicking the trigger button, where the outside-click handler updates the visual state but was never wired to also flip `aria-expanded` back to `false`.

The result is a component that looks completely correct visually and fails a screen reader user in a way that's invisible to anyone testing by sight — the trigger claims `aria-expanded="true"` for a menu that's no longer even in the DOM, so a screen reader user tabs back to the trigger, hears "expanded," and has no idea the menu already closed.

The defense against this isn't more ARIA, it's centralizing the state update: every code path that changes whether the menu is open should flow through one function that updates both the visual state and the ARIA attribute together, so there's no path where one changes without the other. Treat ARIA sync bugs as a state-management problem, not a markup problem.

A few properties apply broadly across many widget types and are worth knowing beyond the role-specific ones already covered:

- **`aria-label`** — provides an accessible name directly as a string, for elements with no visible text (an icon-only close button: `<button aria-label="Close">×</button>`).
- **`aria-labelledby`** — points to the id of another element whose text content becomes this element's accessible name; preferred over `aria-label` when visible text already exists, so the label isn't duplicated in two places that could drift apart.
- **`aria-describedby`** — adds supplementary description (not the name) — commonly used for associating an error message or hint text with a form field.
- **`aria-controls`** — declares that this element controls the visibility/state of another element by id, used alongside `aria-expanded` on things like accordion headers and tab triggers.

The naming distinction between `aria-label`/`aria-labelledby` (the *name* — what is this?) and `aria-describedby` (the *description* — additional context) matters because screen readers announce them differently and in a specific order; conflating the two produces an accessible name that reads like a paragraph instead of a short identifier.

Automated tools like axe catch a meaningful subset of ARIA problems — invalid role/attribute combinations, a role requiring a state that's entirely missing, contrast issues on the labels themselves — but they structurally cannot catch the staleness bug from earlier in this topic, because from a static snapshot, `aria-expanded="true"` looks perfectly valid whether or not it currently matches reality.

The check that actually catches staleness: open the browser devtools Accessibility panel (or the Elements panel's Accessibility tab), watch a specific attribute's value live, and interact with the component through every path a real user might use — not just the happy path of open-via-trigger, close-via-trigger, but also close-via-outside-click, close-via-Escape, close-via-selecting-an-option — confirming the attribute flips correctly on every single one.

A screen reader pass (VoiceOver, NVDA) on the same set of interaction paths is the final, most reliable check, since it's the actual consumer of the attribute and will surface a mismatch a static inspection might not make obvious.

"Make this custom dropdown accessible" as a live exercise is testing the whole chapter at once: does the trigger have `aria-expanded` and `aria-haspopup`, does it toggle correctly on every close path (not just the trigger), is the menu itself reachable and operable by keyboard (arrow keys to move between options, Enter to select, Escape to close and return focus to the trigger), and does the selected/highlighted option get communicated to a screen reader via `aria-activedescendant` or actual DOM focus movement.

A candidate who adds `role="listbox"`/`role="option"` and stops there has covered the *labeling* half of the problem but not the *interaction* half — a screen reader will now correctly announce it as a listbox, but a keyboard user still can't operate it unless the arrow-key and Escape handling is separately implemented. Both halves are required; ARIA roles alone never add keyboard behavior — that's still on you to build.

A complete answer about ARIA in an interview covers four things, in order: **when to use it** (only when no native element covers the interaction), **what it actually provides** (a promise to assistive tech about role/state/properties — never automatic behavior), **the sync obligation** (every state attribute must be updated through every code path that changes the real UI, not just the obvious one), and **its limits** (it never adds keyboard handling, focus management, or any interaction logic on its own).

The candidates who miss points here usually say "add ARIA labels" as if that's a complete accessibility fix for a custom widget — it's necessary but nowhere near sufficient, since the keyboard interaction and state-sync work is the harder, larger half of making a custom component actually accessible, not an afterthought to the labeling.
